definition: Embezzle means to steal money entrusted to one's care by falsifying records.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word embezzle. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know embezzle should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The mill's payroll clerk embezzled for years by keeping a retired welder on the books and pocketing each ghost paycheck.
Pilfer is petty and opportunistic — pens from the supply closet; it stops far short of embezzle's engineered scheme.
Skim comes closer — quietly shaving cash off the day's take — but it still stops short of embezzle, which rewrites the books themselves to bury a larger theft.

Misappropriate is the broad legal term for putting entrusted money or property to your own use, and it covers careless misuse as well as outright theft. Embezzle is its narrower, harsher cousin: the trusted insider not only takes the funds but falsifies the records to hide the taking.

Siphon means to drain money off little by little through a hidden channel — the picture is a slow, quiet leak. Embezzle can involve siphoning, but it adds the legal core: the money was entrusted to your care, and the books are doctored to cover the loss.

Besiller left no other offspring in English — embezzle is the family's sole survivor. The prefix is real, but there is no root to reuse, so learn the word whole and let the em- remind you that the thief is on the inside.
Embezzle means to steal money entrusted to one's care by falsifying records.
The hotel's night manager embezzled quietly for a decade: he voided one room charge each evening, took the cash himself, and initialed the register so the shortfall never showed.
Embezzle is narrower than steal.

A burglar takes what was never his to touch; an embezzler is the trusted insider — the clerk, the manager, the keeper of the accounts — who is handed the money legitimately and then quietly rewrites the records to keep it.
Embezzle is the precise word when a trusted insider steals funds and doctors the records; courts, auditors, and reporters all reach for it.
If the money was grabbed rather than entrusted, it is theft or robbery, not embezzlement — and misappropriate covers sloppier misuse of entrusted property that stops short of outright stealing.

For six years, the aquarium's finance director was the person trustees praised most: bills paid early, budgets balanced to the dollar.
Then a new bank portal showed a trustee the raw statements, and the balancing act collapsed.
The director had been paying a real cleaning company $4,000 a month, recording $9,000, and moving the difference into an account under her cousin's name.
Because she controlled both the payments and the reports, no one had ever compared the two.
At trial, the word prosecutors used was embezzle: she had not broken in from outside but had stolen money already placed in her hands, rewriting the records to hide it.
